PHOENIX -- Varias latas de cerveza fueron vaciadas sobre la cabeza de Aaron Judge mientras el capitán de los Yankees permanecía en el centro del clubhouse de visitantes en el Target Field la semana pasada, rodeado de compañeros eufóricos que celebraban la clasificación del club a la postemporada.
Judge entrecerró los ojos por el ardor y les advirtió a sus compañeros: “Me las van a pagar”.
Aun así, no pretenden que ésa sea su última celebración, pues tienen un firme control del primer puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana y el título del Este de la Liga Americana todavía está en juego.
“Siempre es bueno cuando puedes celebrar esos momentos durante una temporada”, dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. “Mucha gente dedica mucho tiempo, esfuerzo y sudor. Obviamente, éste es apenas el primer paso de lo que esperamos sean muchos”.
Ahora que aseguraron su pase a la postemporada, ¿qué más les espera a los Yankees?
¿Cómo podría quedar el roster para la postemporada?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez 
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Trent Grisham, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos
BD: Ben Rice
LA: Gerrit Cole, Cam Schlittler, Max Fried
R: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber, Will Warren, Carlos Rodón
Los Yankees utilizaron a 12 lanzadores y a 14 bateadores cuando recibieron a los Medias Rojas en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, así que partiremos de esa misma premisa para el 2026.
Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles contra Tampa Bay, mientras que Schlittler lo hará el jueves. Mirando hacia adelante, eso sugiere que Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Es posible que los Yankees estén alineando a Cole para abrir el Juego 1 y a Schlittler para el Juego 2. Hasta ahora, han preferido no decir mucho al respecto, salvo por la confirmación de Boone de que Cole realizará una apertura en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Rodón podría estar en el bullpen para la serie. En nuestra proyección del roster lo tenemos activo, mientras que el dominicano Luis Gil y Ryan Yarbrough figuran entre quienes quedarían fuera. Ryan Weathers trabaja para regresar como relevista, pero el tiempo juega en su contra. Si está saludable, podría ocupar el lugar de Fulmer o Schreiber.
Chisholm espera regresar esta semana para la serie contra los Rays tras sufrir un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Grisham ha mostrado mejoría y podría quedarse con un puesto en los jardines. De no ser así, Max Schuemann está entre las alternativas. Otro aspecto para seguir: ¿Podrían los Yankees incluir a Anthony Volpe en lugar de Rosario? Es una posibilidad que vale la pena considerar.
¿Cuándo comenzará la postemporada?
Si los Yankees terminan disputando la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, ésta empezará el 29 de septiembre. La Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana arrancará el 3 de octubre.
¿Contra quién jugarían los Yankees si la temporada terminara hoy?
En estos momentos, sería una revancha de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, con los Yankees recibiendo a los Medias Rojas en el Bronx. Los Yankees ganaron aquella serie dos victorias por una.
Este año, los Yankees tuvieron marca de 7-6 contra Boston.
¿Todavía pueden ganar el Este de la Liga Americana?
Sí, pero tienen un camino cuesta arriba. Los Yankees tienen por delante cuatro enfrentamientos directos con los Rays a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium, incluyendo una doble-cartelera para abrir la serie. Tampa Bay domina actualmente la serie particular por 6-3, lo que significa que los Yankees necesitarían barrer para quedarse con el criterio de desempate entre ambos.
¿Quién abriría el Juego 1 por los Yankees?
Como se mencionó anteriormente, Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles frente a Tampa Bay y Schlittler lo hará al día siguiente. Por lo tanto, Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Después de permitir siete jonrones en sus dos aperturas anteriores, Cole mermó las dudas externas sobre una posible apertura en los playoffs con una sólida actuación en Arizona. Fried y Rodón han lidiado con lesiones, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado.
Warren realizará una apertura más durante la serie contra los Orioles, según Boone, pero llegará a los playoffs como una interesante alternativa para el relevo.
¿Será Judge un factor en los playoffs?
Los Yankees han sido poco específicos sobre el estado de Judge. Boone ha evitado ofrecer un plazo estimado para su recuperación e incluso revelar el grado del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha. En términos generales, hasta un tirón de Grado 1, el de menor gravedad, requiere de dos a tres semanas para una recuperación completa.
Es casi seguro que Judge intentará regresar antes. La primera fecha en la que podría ser activado sería para el Juego 162, el 27 de septiembre. Tal como está el panorama ahora mismo, existe una posibilidad muy real de que los Yankees no cuenten con Judge al menos para una potencial Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Judge dijo que le “gustaría” estar activo para la postemporada y que ése es “el plan”, pero no dijo necesariamente que sería para el 29 de septiembre.
¿Cuáles son las otras preocupaciones en cuanto a lesiones?
Grisham ha avanzado en su programa progresivo de correr y debe de estar disponible para el roster de los playoffs, aunque Boone dijo que no será activado antes de que termine la temporada regular. Chisholm ha estado bateando y realizando tiros, y debe de ser activado durante la serie contra los Rays. Si sufre algún contratiempo, Volpe entraría en consideración.
Y aunque los Yankees no han descartado a Giancarlo Stanton, quien ha estado bateando, han ofrecido pocas novedades sobre su recuperación del más reciente tirón en la pantorrilla.

- It’s a fool’s errand, but here’s one last update for the final week of the season. I tried emphasizing two-start starters unless they’re particularly dangerous, but I also tried to take into account that some of the guys currently in line to start twice are going to end up being scratched or making only brief appearances next weekend.
- With no updates yet on Alex Bregman (face) and Andrés Muñoz (knee), I’ve dropped both from the rankings. Pedro Ramírez, who was set to fall off the list with Dansby Swanson back, reclaimed a spot in Bregman’s place. - Thank you so much to everyone who has followed along all season. Anyone interested in the full spreadsheet of where players have ranked start to finish, reach out to my gmail at matthewpouliot. I’ll be back in mid-October with the first (or second) go at a 2027 Top 300.

September 7 Notes

Also, Athletics hitters have moved up, since they’ll be at home for six games this week. Rockies hitters have dropped off as that team goes back on the road after a week of home games.

Amazing is the consistency in his wOBAs since 2021: .373, .373, .359, .364, .365 and .365. His xwOBAs, on the other hand, still show a little decline: .391, .365, .380, .366, .367, .340. In the end, he didn’t quite make the cut. It will be really interesting to see how the Brewers play things the rest of the way. San Diego’s Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, at least made it up to 4 1/3 innings in his last rehab start as he returns from an elbow injury. That gets him a spot on the bottom of the list, even if he’s a long shot to get a win Monday in his return.

The New York Yankees won't win the American League East after dropping two out of three games to the Arizona Diamondbacks and are now looking at another Wild Card series against the Boston Red Sox. The rest of this season will now be about figuring out their roster heading into October, and this Rays series won't mean much.
There are plenty of questions from fans about what the roster should look like in the final week of the season. And if you're curious about that, reach out to Joseph Randazzo on X or Instagram at @YankeeLibrarian. Fans can ask anything, from questions about bullpen trust trees to what to do with Jazz Chisholm Jr. when he's activated.
The state of the bullpen
Who do you trust in the bullpen outside of Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, and David Bednar?@Mattmann1199 on Instagram
At this point, the two best names behind them are Will Warren and John Schreiber. It's likely that they'll be without Ryan Weathers, and that is the name I would have gone with. Now it's probably Schreiber, but I'm not too convinced about this answer.
Since Luis Gil has been blowing 100 out of the bullpen, they can see what they have in him as a pen arm heading into October. None of these answers inspire much, but they have somehow been one of the best bullpens in baseball.
A returning bat
Where should Jazz Chisholm Jr. play when they activate him@theezratakeshita on Instagram
Chisholm should probably go to second base. Volpe has been okay, but since his big debut against the Colorado Rockies, he has gone 7-for-33. He has two doubles, three stolen bases, and two RBI.
Since Boston has a ton of lefty starters, they can probably start a game with Volpe and then go to Chisholm later. That feels like what the Yankees will do, and it's probably the case if Volpe is scorching the ball. Of course, there is still time for Volpe to make things interesting here.
Judge's World Series dreams
The World Series window for Judge is closing. Might he go without ever winning one?@_not_mikeee on Instagram
That is absolutely on the table. There are some great players who have never won a championship. Dan Marino, Barry Bonds, and Henrik Lundqvist never got their ring. Granted, the Scott Hunter character in Heated Rivalry feels like it's loosely based on mid-2010s Lundqvist, but that might only half-count since it's a work of fiction.
A wild storyline would be the Yankees winning a World Series this year without Judge. Imagine the chaos of his legacy talks if that happens.
Job statuses
Is there a scenario that gets Cash or Boone fired this year?@kirby.phillips7 on Instagram
These questions are always easy to answer. Probably not this year. Cashman will probably go out on his own accord. Boone is the most likely candidate to get fired, but there aren't many teams that are going to axe a manager who kept their team afloat and in postseason contention with the amount of injuries they had. When baseball comes back after the lockout, those two will probably still be here.
Missing the playoffs again might do it for them, but the last time that happened, they stayed. It does feel like they have unlimited security in New York.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.
Pitchers (11): Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Clarke Schmidt, John Schreiber, Tim Hill, Ryan Weathers
As things stand, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are scheduled to pitch against the Rays, in that order. That would give Cole, who has struggled to get swing-and-miss, an extra day of rest if he were to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young frontrunner, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1.
Because the Wild Card round is a best-of-three series, Rodón isn’t needed, especially with Will Warren expected to work out of the bullpen and able to provide length.
Warren, slated to make one more start this season after struggling on Sunday, is one of a few converted starters who could impact the Bombers’ bullpen this postseason. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are the others. Schmidt, being cautious in his return from Tommy John surgery, couldn’t come into Sunday’s game due to some bicep cramping, while Weathers isn’t expected to return from a flexor strain before the regular season ends.
Still, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled out the idea of Weathers’ first game back coming in the playoffs.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”
As for the relievers that the Yankees have leaned on all season, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick headline the group. All have been used heavily, especially Headrick.
The lefty allowed a grand slam to Nolan Arenado and saw his fastball velocity down an average of 1.3 mph during his major league-leading 79th appearance on Sunday, but he insisted that he feels fine physically. Boone also downplayed concerns over Headrick’s ongoing velocity fluctuations, though he did say that he hopes to get him and other relievers “in a good spot” with some rest ahead of the playoffs.
That said, the Yankees still haven’t been eliminated from the AL East race. They’ll keep trying to take the division from the Rays until they are.
“We’re going to show up Tuesday,” Boone said, “and try and kick their butt.”

item.content:encoded:
It's no secret that Yankees left-handed relief pitcher Brent Headrick has been one of, if not their most dominant relief pitcher this season in 2026. However, concerns are growing about Brent Headrick as we approach the final week of the regular season before the postseason.
Yankees beat writer Brendan Kuty of The Athletic posted earlier this evening in a tweet that "Headrick's average fastball velocity tonight in Arizona against the Diamondbacks was 92.9 mph, which Kuty cites as 1.3 mph slower than his 'season average of 94.2 mph."
Headrick Gave Up Grand Slam In 8-4 Loss In Arizona
Headrick came into this game with the bases loaded and two outs; he proceeded to walk in a run facing right fielder Corbin Caroll, and then gave up a grand slam to D-Backs third baseman Nolan Arenado to go from a 4-1 Yankees lead to then a 6-4 D-Backs lead, a game in which they would go on to win 8-4. Oddly enough, the pitch before Arenado just pulled foul down the left field line, only to hit a grand slam that stayed fair on the very next pitch to left field.
Headrick has been phenomenal this year with a 7-4 record and a 2.10 ERA in 79 appearances. His ERA has been under 2 for much of the season, but in his last seven games, he's struggled with a 4.76 ERA in 5.2 innings of work. However, for much of the 2026 season, Headrick's ERA has been under two. The concerning part is that Headrick looks worn out. Pitching in so many crucial games this year, when the Yankees were tied or in a close game, has forced the organization to rely on Headrick a lot.
It makes sense why Headrick's velocity, therefore, would be down a bit, per Kuty's tweet. If the Yankees want to win a World Series, they will need not only significant contributions from key players in the lineup, but also from the bullpen, on which they've relied heavily: the trio of closer David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, and Brent Headrick.
Headrick's breakout 2026 campaign with the Yankees and his story are a rather interesting one. The Yankees claimed Brent Headrick off waivers in February 2025 from the Minnesota Twins. Before joining the Yankees, Headrick pitched to a 5.97 ERA with the Twins in 15 games spanning 2023-24.
Yankees Likely To Rest Headrick Before Playoffs
Headrick's usage for the rest of the regular season and then the postseason, likely a Wild Card matchup between the Yankees and Red Sox, will be something to monitor moving forward. If the Yankees want to win a World Series this year, they will have to rely heavily on Brent Headrick, as they have throughout the 2026 season, to get an opportunity in the postseason.
The challenge will also be longer, since the Yankees will likely have to come out of the Wild Card. The Yankees now have their final two regular-season matchups: four games against the Tampa Bay Rays, then three against the Baltimore Orioles. The Wild Card series begins on Tuesday, September 29th, as the Yankees will look for more of the Brent Headrick they've seen for much of the 2026 season and not the version they saw of him today.

It’s Sunday once more, and you know what that means — it’s time for our weekly social media roundup! This weekend has been yet another veritable whirlwind in the Bronx, as the team celebrated a postseason appearance, bid farewell to a fan favorite, closed an era of minor league baseball, and watched as their Captain hit the shelf once more. With so much in store, let’s get started!
Another Celebration in Minnesota
It was deja vu all over again! For what feels like the fifty millionth time, the Yankees celebrated in Minnesota, as they clinched a postseason berth earlier this week with a victory over their favorite AL Central punching bag.
The Roberto Clemente Award
This week, the New York Yankees named Carlos Rodón their nominee for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award. The team honored the Rodón Foundation, which sets out to help families suffering with fertility issues.
In Service
Yankees reliever Brent Headrick welcomed Henry Ledlowe from his hometown in Illinois to the Bronx, courtesy of the National Down Syndrome Society. Unfortunately, the Instagram post cannot be embedded, but can be found here.
The Jazz Chisholm Jr. Foundation, meanwhile, marked the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
Where’s Oswaldo? Unfortunately, Cincy.
This week, the Yankees designated fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment in order to make room on the 40-man roster for Clarke Schmidt. Unfortunately, he was claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Reds, and while we’re all excited to see him (hopefully) get some regular playing time — as he was very much blocked in the Bronx — it will be sad to see the human golden retriever, well-loved by the fans and players alike, in a different uniform.
A testament to his popularity is the fact that the Yankees, RailRiders, Patriots, and YES Network all posted farewells to him on their social media accounts. David Cone also came back to Twitter briefly in order to wish him well.
Farewell to the RailRiders
Starting next year, the Yankees’ Triple-A affiliate will undergo its second rebrand since joining the Yankees family, abandoning the RailRider moniker in exchange for a new nickname which has yet to be revealed. To honor the end of the era, Clint Frazier — who self-identifies as a Scranton RailRider more than anyone else in baseball — threw out the ceremonial first pitch prior to their final game.
Road Trip Nonsense
Meredith Marakovitz, Suzyn Waldman, and Dave Simms always have fun on the road trips, and this one is no different!
The Knicks are Back
This week, the Yankees will be hosting Josh Hart bobblehead night, celebrating the 2026 NBA Champion (and 2016 NCAA Champion!) who is related to Yankees legend Elston Howard. Fun fact — this has been scheduled since last year, so it actually predates the Knicks’ championship; what fantastic luck for the marketing team!
Celebrating Howie
Last Sunday, Mets broadcaster Howie Rose called his last game at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees set out to make the day special, and many of his friends and coworkers in the Yankees broadcast teams celebrated his career with him.
Official Videos
First, the latest episode of Behind the NY gives us a behind-the scenes look at the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
Then, we got a behind-the-scenes look of David Bednar entering the game on Sunday.
Last, but not least, we have Cody Bellinger talking about his story.
We’ve got a special edition of this week’s Question of the Day, as we not only have the Yankees answering questions, we’ve got the Somerset Patriots reading Thank You Cards as they wrap up their season.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se pasaron casi toda la noche del sábado lidiando con dos realidades en el Chase Field. Cam Schlittler volvió a ofrecerles una gran salida, pero cada entrada cobró más importancia después de que Tampa Bay ya se hubiera llevado la victoria con un tanto decisivo en la última entrada.
Nueva York tuvo la oportunidad de evitar que sus cada vez más remotas opciones en la División Este de la Liga Americana se le escaparan aún más. En cambio, los Yankees se fueron con una derrota por 5-3 ante los Diamondbacks de Arizona, lo que amplió su desventaja en la división a cinco partidos cuando solo quedan ocho por disputar.
Los Yankees hicieron lo suficiente para que el partido se pudiera ganar. Ben Rice conectó un fly de sacrificio en la quinta entrada. Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells conectaron jonrones en la sexta. Schlittler superó su primer bajón serio en el control en semanas y terminó seis entradas concediendo solo una carrera limpia.
Arizona siguió respondiendo. Jordan Lawlar neutralizó la primera ventaja de Nueva York con un triple de dos carreras en la quinta entrada, después de que Schlittler fallara al intentar atrapar un toque. Corbin Carroll empató el partido con un fly de sacrificio en la sexta entrada, tras dos bases por bolas y un sencillo de toque que llenaron las bases.
Lo que estaba en juego ya estaba claro antes del primer lanzamiento. Varios jugadores de los Yankees vieron desde el vestuario de visitantes cómo Tampa Bay vencía a Boston por 2-1, un resultado que situaba a los Rays cinco partidos por delante. Nueva York había ganado ocho de sus últimos diez partidos, pero la racha de Tampa Bay casi no dejaba margen para perder otra oportunidad.
A continuación, los Yankees contaron con dos entradas sin puntos de su bullpen. Brent Headrick consiguió dos outs en la séptima antes de que Paul Blackburn terminara esa entrada y se encargara de la octava. El marcador se mantuvo en 3-3, lo que dejaba a Nueva York a una entrada limpia de tener otra oportunidad al bate.
Schlittler había hecho lo suficiente para mantener a los Yankees en el partido. Cedió tres hits y tres carreras, solo una limpia, y se anotó seis strikeouts en 98 lanzamientos. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó a 1,94. Para entonces, el margen de error era ya casi nulo.
Fue entonces cuando el partido dio un giro con la decisión más decisiva de Aaron Boone de toda la noche respecto al bullpen.
Boone recurre a Fulmer con el partido en juego
Boone le pasó la parte baja de la novena a Michael Fulmer en lugar de al cerrador David Bednar. Fulmer había lanzado dos tercios de una entrada sin encajar carreras en la victoria del viernes por 9-2, mientras que Bednar no había lanzado desde que hizo dos entradas el miércoles en Minnesota.
Fulmer parecía haber eliminado a Ildemaro Vargas con un strikeout en un lanzamiento con cuenta completa, pero Vargas impugnó la decisión a través del sistema automático de bolas y strikes de la MLB. El lanzamiento se consideró bola, lo que le dio a Arizona una base por bolas para abrir el turno.
Fulmer ponchó a Lawlar. A continuación, Pavin Smith entró como bateador suplente y mandó el segundo lanzamiento de Fulmer, un «cutter», 391 pies al campo derecho para un jonrón de dos carreras que dio la victoria.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria para Arizona, mejorando su balance a 5-4. Fulmer sufrió su primera derrota y vio cómo su promedio de carreras limpias subía de 1,59 a 3,09. No hubo salvamento.
La decisión llamó la atención porque Bednar llegaba a la noche con 34 salvamentos y una efectividad de 2,58. Fulmer, fichado por los Yankees a finales de agosto, solo había lanzado 11 1/3 entradas en las Grandes Ligas esta temporada antes del sábado y sigue formando parte de un bullpen muy concurrido de la postemporada.
Schlittler asume la culpa tras una racha irregular
Un error de Schlittler en la quinta entrada ayudó a Arizona a anotar dos veces, y ocho lanzamientos seguidos fuera de la zona al inicio de la sexta propiciaron la remontada que empató el partido. Se recuperó ponchando a Nolan Arenado y a Tim Tawa con dos corredores en posición de anotar.
El lanzador diestro se centró en su propio error tras el partido.
«Asumo toda la culpa por eso», dijo Schlittler. «Cometí un error ahí y dejé que nos marcaran dos carreras. Así es el béisbol, pero esa la tengo yo».
Schlittler ha cedido una carrera limpia o menos en 24 salidas como titular, lo que le convierte, junto a Sandy Koufax y Bob Gibson, en uno de los únicos lanzadores de la Era de la Bola Viva con al menos 24 salidas de este tipo en una temporada, sin contar los «openers».
El descanso de Bednar acentúa el contraste en el bullpen
La secuencia de relevos de los Yankees ofreció un anticipo de la postemporada. Headrick y Blackburn sumaron entre ambos dos entradas sin encajar carreras antes de la novena. Bednar no llegó a salir, mientras que Fulmer lanzó dos días seguidos.
Fulmer llegaba al sábado con una ERA de 1,59 y había limitado a sus rivales a un promedio de bateo de 0,171 en sus apariciones con los Yankees. La diferencia en la carga de trabajo era aún más marcada: Fulmer había lanzado el viernes, mientras que Bednar había tenido dos días completos de descanso tras su salida de dos entradas del miércoles.
Esto es importante ahora que los Yankees están reorganizando una plantilla de lanzadores que se reducirá de cara a octubre. Bednar es una opción consolidada para las últimas entradas. Fulmer ha lanzado lo suficientemente bien como para seguir en la pugna por un puesto en la plantilla, pero su puesto está menos asegurado, ya que varios relevistas compiten por las limitadas plazas de la postemporada.
El sábado supuso otro momento de evaluación, y esta vez se dio en un momento de máxima presión.
Los Yankees pierden más terreno antes del enfrentamiento con los Rays
Con esta derrota, los Yankees se quedan con un balance de 89-65. Tampa Bay sube a 94-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a cinco partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees siguen teniendo una ventaja de 5 partidos y medio sobre Boston en la lucha por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Boone reconoció lo estrecho que se ha vuelto el camino con cuatro partidos contra Tampa Bay a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium.
«Si les barreríamos, entonces la cosa se pondría interesante», dijo Boone. «Pero no puedes barrerlos antes del partido [del domingo]».
Los Yankees cierran la serie contra Arizona el domingo, con Will Warren como lanzador previsto para enfrentarse a Corbin Burnes. Tras el partido del sábado, Nueva York debe mantener viva la lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, decidir en qué relevos confía Boone cuando llegue la próxima novena entrada empatada.

Seattle, Washington.- Cam Schlittler lanzó un juego sin permitir carreras hasta la séptima entrada y Paul Goldschmidt conectó un jonrón de tres carreras, lo que permitió a los Yankees de Nueva York vencer a los Marineros de Seattle por 5-3 el miércoles.
Ben Rice también conectó un jonrón y un doble productor para los Yankees, que terminaron con un récord de 5-1 en su gira por la Costa Oeste al inicio de la temporada. Jugarán su primer partido en casa el viernes contra los Miami Marlins.
Schlittler (2-0) permitió dos hits en 6 1/3 entradas y retiró a sus últimos 16 bateadores, extendiendo su inicio de temporada sin permitir carreras. Ponchó a siete y no otorgó bases por bolas en 79 lanzamientos, 58 de ellos strikes.
El lanzador derecho de 25 años dejó a los Giants sin carreras durante 5 1/3 entradas el viernes pasado. Solo ha permitido tres hits esta temporada, mientras que ha ponchado a 15 bateadores. Tanto él como su compañero Max Fried no han permitido carreras en sus dos aperturas esta temporada.
Brendan Donovan abrió la parte baja de la primera entrada con un doble, pero fue el único jugador que llegó a segunda base contra Schlittler.
David Bednar necesitó 40 lanzamientos para conseguir los cuatro outs y lograr su tercer salvamento.
Nueva York tomó la delantera en la primera entrada con un doble productor de Rice, y Goldschmidt conectó un jonrón contra el abridor George Kirby (1-1) en la sexta entrada, su primer jonrón de la temporada. Fue el primer jonrón de Goldschmidt contra un lanzador diestro desde el 6 de junio.
Rice añadió un jonrón solitario en la novena entrada, su primer jonrón del año.
Cal Raleigh impulsó dos carreras para Seattle con un sencillo de bate roto ante Bednar con dos outs en la octava entrada, reduciendo la desventaja a 4-2. Dominic Canzone conectó un sencillo productor de carrera en la novena entrada.
Desde el partido del lunes por la noche, los lanzadores abridores de los Yankees no han permitido ninguna carrera en 16 entradas consecutivas.
A continuación
El lanzador derecho de los Yankees, Will Warren (0-0), abrirá el viernes contra el lanzador derecho de los Marlins, Eury Pérez (0-0).
El lanzador derecho de los Mariners, Bryan Woo (0-0), recibirá la pelota el viernes por la noche como visitante contra el lanzador zurdo de los Angels de Los Ángeles, Reid Detmers (0-0).

item.content:encoded:
Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). Captain Aaron Judge is less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him more than three months. Judge's status for the rest of the season is up in the air.
"I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires," manager Aaron Boone said (via MLB.com). "... The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
The Yankees are always cagey about Judge's injuries. They declined to reveal the severity of the calf strain or give a timetable for his return. Generally speaking, Grade 1 calf strains (the least severe) require 2-3 weeks on the injured list, though calves are very tricky and easy to reinjury. They must be allowed to heal fully, otherwise you risk a more severe injury.
For all intents and purposes, the Yankees are locked into the top wild-card spot. They're six games up in the loss column on the Boston Red Sox, who currently sit in the second wild card spot, plus the Yankees won the season series and have the tiebreaker, so it's really a seven-game lead. New York can clinch the top wild-card spot as soon as Sunday.
The AL East title remains mathematically possible, but it is a long shot. The Yankees are four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the loss column with four head-to-head games remaining next week in the Bronx. The Rays only need to win one of those four games to clinch the season series and secure the tiebreaker, upping the difficulty for New York.
Just to lay it all out, here's what needs to happen for the Yankees to win the AL East, assuming they sweep those four games against the Rays and clinch the tiebreaker for themselves, which is a pretty big assumption:
- Rays go 6-3 or better: Rays win AL East
- Rays go 5-4: Yankees must go 9-0
- Rays go 4-5: Yankees must go 8-1
- Rays go 3-6: Yankees must go 7-2
- Rays go 2-7: Yankees must go 6-3
- Rays go 1-8: Yankees must go 5-4
- Rays go 0-9: Yankees must go 4-5
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason spot and winning the AL East was a long shot even with Judge. These last nine regular-season games are almost meaningless. If the AL East race gets interesting in a few days, the Yankees can shift gears, but the big picture takes priority this next week. Resting key relievers, lining up the rotation for the Wild Card Series, etc.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game," Cody Bellinger said (via MLB.com). "For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I'm fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody."
With the postseason less than two weeks away, Judge's calf injury creates a lot of questions for both him and the Yankees overall. Here are three questions for the man himself, and his team.
Three questions for Judge
1. Will he return for the postseason? This is really the only question, right? The Yankees are built around Judge being the best hitter in the world, and when he's not, the walls begin to cave in. New York had one of the lowest-scoring offenses in baseball when Judge was out with his rib injury. To paraphrase another New York baseball legend, Judge is the straw that stirs the drink.
Judge is eligible to come off the injured list next Sunday, the final day of the regular season. Roster-wise, he can return in time for the postseason. Health-wise, we have no idea. Calf strains are rarely 10-day absences, but that's what the Yankees have to hope is the case here. There's a very real chance the Yankees are without Judge for at least the Wild Card Series, and maybe longer.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Aaron Judge said. “That’s definitely the plan.”
Said the calf strain involves the soleus muscle — which he said is more crucial to running and hitting — making it more difficult to play through.
2. Will he be himself at the plate? Judge did not go on a minor-league rehab assignment before returning from the rib injury and it showed. He went 4 for 23 (.174) with one walk and 13 strikeouts in his seven games back before the calf injury. His timing was not there at all. Judge's one homer came on a hanging breaking ball. Otherwise, pitchers threw fastballs by him consistently.
To put a number on it, Judge missed with 41% of his swings against fastballs in his seven games back, more than double the 19% league average. This is what it looks like when you miss with more than two out of every five swings against heaters:
It is not exactly a surprise a hitter who did not go on a rehab assignment after spending more than three months on the shelf looked out of sorts at the plate. Judge and the Yankees knew it would take him some time to get back up to speed at the plate, and they were willing to live with it. The goal was always to be ready for the postseason, not so much the regular season.
These last nine games aren't particularly important for the Yankees in the standings, but they were incredibly important to Judge. He needed at-bats to rediscover his timing at the plate, and get back to being the dominant hitter he's been throughout his career. The calf strain puts that on pause. Judge now has even fewer at-bats available to get back to being himself.
3. Will he be able to play the field? There is a scenario in which Judge plays through the calf strain as a full-time DH who doesn't run at 100% (or close to it). How the Yankees would align their defense in that scenario, I have no idea. Ben Rice is a full-time DH these days and also New York's best non-Judge hitter. Platoon-mates Luis Gárcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt are first basemen.
Unless the Yankees do something unexpected, like put Gárcia back at second base (where he was terrible defensively) or Rice back behind the plate (where he was also terrible defensively), slotting Judge in at DH means one of the team's most productive hitters will have to sit. This is something the Yankees will worry about when the time comes, and not a second sooner.
Three questions for the Yankees
1. Where will the righty pop come from? The Yankees have a very lefty-heavy lineup and Judge's righty heft provides important balance. Only the Cleveland Guardians have gotten fewer plate appearances from righties this season. Friday's lineup against Arizona Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez could be what the Yankees run out there against lefties in October:
- 1B Paul Goldschmidt, RHB
- LF Cody Bellinger, LHB
- RF Heliot Ramos, RHB
- DH Ben Rice, LHB
- 3B Amed Rosario, RHB
- CF Spencer Jones, LHB
- SS George Lombard Jr., RHB
- C Austin Wells, LHB
- 2B Anthony Volpe, RHB
Goldschmidt and Ramos are lefty mashers. Bellinger and Rice are very productive left-on-left hitters. Jones has performed well against lefties as a big leaguer, though his minor-league track record against southpaws isn't great. Rosario is having his worst season against lefties. The 7-8-9 spots are unlikely to make an impact offensively, regardless of the pitcher's handedness.
That lineup would look much more imposing with Judge in the No. 3 spot. Perhaps this is not such a big concern though? Since trade deadline day, the Yankees have the highest batting average (.289) and on-base percentage (.362) against lefties, and the third-highest slugging percentage (.456) despite Judge not playing much, and not being much of a factor when he did play.
In all likelihood the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and Boston has three quality lefty starters (Jake Bennett, Ranger Suárez, Payton Tolle) and a shutdown lefty relief tandem (Aroldis Chapman, Erik Miller). To beat the Red Sox, the Yankees will need their righty hitters to produce, and now the status of their best right-handed hitter is in question.
2. Will the pitching hold up? Despite not having Judge for more than three months, the Yankees have the American League's best run differential (+143) and second-best record (89-64). They can thank their pitching staff. New York has allowed only 3.68 runs per game this year, the fewest in baseball. Since trade deadline day, it's an incredible 3.37 runs allowed per game.
There are some cracks beginning to form, however. Gerrit Cole has surrendered eight home runs in his last three starts, including five on a four-seam fastball that is no longer the dominant pitch it was at his peak. Max Fried's velocity has been down a tick since returning from a bone bruise in his elbow late last month. That injury has sent him to the injured list twice this year.
Cam Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, has thrown a career-high 184 ⅔ innings with two regular-season starts remaining, plus the postseason. Key late-inning relievers Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, and Brent Headrick have worked a lot -- A LOT -- this season and have all shown a slight dip in velocity in recent weeks, which perhaps is a sign the workload is catching up to them.
Without Judge (and sometimes even with him), the Yankees are a run prevention team. Their superpower is a suffocating pitching staff that is among the best in baseball at limiting hard contact, particularly in the air. With Judge absent, the pitching staff and the ability to prevent runs in general will be of paramount importance. No Judge reduces the margin of error considerably.
3. What about their other injured players? Judge is not the only injured Yankee. Center field Trent Grisham has not played since Sept. 4 due to a Grade 2 hamstring strain. On Friday, Boone said Grisham is pretty far into his running program, and he could make it back before the end of the regular season. That would give the outfield a lift should Judge miss extended time.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. has not played since jamming his thumb sliding into second base on Sept. 8. Boone said Chisholm will come off the injured list when the Yankees return home next week. He's had a down year overall, but Chisholm was playing his best baseball of the season right before the injury. He's an important presence given his speed and defense in particular.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers is working his way back from a flexor strain. He last pitched Aug. 22. Weathers is throwing bullpen sessions, though Boone confirmed he won't return during the regular season. If/when Weathers does return, it will be as a reliever. He has bullpen experience and the Yankees could use middle relief help, but Weathers has to make it back first.
At minimum, Chisholm and Grisham would give the Yankees more options for their Judge-less lineup, even if they only platoon. It wouldn't be hard to find a role for Weathers, who had allowed no more than one run in six of his last seven starts before the injury. Bottom line though, the Yankees need Judge. Everything else is secondary to his return and effectiveness.

The New York Yankees could make a surprising move on Anthony Volpe.
Volpe has had success since being recalled, but George Lombard Jr. has taken over as the starting shortstop. So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air.
New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.
New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision
Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.
After New York clinched a playoff spot, Yankees analysts Bryan Hoch and Patrick Donnelly of MLB.com revealed the likely playoff roster, and they didn't have Volpe on it.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Aaron Judge, Heliot Ramos
DH: Ben Rice
SP: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
RP: David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren
The Yankees leaving Volpe off the playoff roster would be a disappointing outcome for the shortstop. It also could signal the end of his tenure in New York as Lombard is the shortstop of the future.
Volpe is hitting .253 with 2 home runs and 26 RBIs this season with the Yankees.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
However, despite clinching a playoff spot, the Yankees made it clear the job isn't finished. New York likely won't win the AL East again, which is frustrating, but the Yankees have confidence they can go on a deep playoff run.
The Yankees are 88-64 and 5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the AL East.

It wasn't all bad news from a discouraging and frustrating 13-inning defeat at the hands of the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon, even if it really, really stung for a number of reasons.
The ray of sunshine in what was a rough day for the Yankees' divisional hopes was the return of someone they view as crucial to their chances at a deep playoff run. After a 440-day absence due to Tommy John surgery, Clarke Schmidt made his Yankees return, tossing two-thirds of an inning in the seventh before being removed due to pitch count.
It wasn't the cleanest outing, as he wasn't able to get through a full inning after throwing 24 pitches to four batters, but for someone on a big league mound for the first time in 14 months, you had to like what you saw, striking out a pair and only surrendering a pair of soft-hit singles.
The runway is rather short for the remainder of the season with just 10 games left, but Schmidt will likely see his way into four or so games down the stretch. That gives him a total of five outings to truly figure out where he can fit into a wide-open bullpen trust tree.
Clarke Schmidt's bullpen experience
Converting a full-time starter to the bullpen is not always as easy as it seems, but it's a transition the Yankees will have to make three times as we head into the postseason, with Ryan Weathers' likely return and Will Warren's place in the rotation. That said, Schmidt has a bit of an advantage.
Before becoming a full-time starter at the major-league level in 2023, Schmidt was used almost exclusively as a reliever in his brief big-league stints, most notably in 2022, when he posted a 3.12 ERA in 57.2 innings as part of a makeshift bullpen that got very good results. He didn't get himself high up the totem pole, but he pitched some important innings for the club.
His playoff experience as a reliever was unfortunately one to forget. He was saddled with a pair of losses, first in Game 3 of the ALDS after a squeaker by Oscar Gonzalez got through the infield for a walk-off single, and the second in Game 1 of the ALCS against the Houston Astros, where he allowed home runs to Yuli Gurriel and Chas McCormick in the sixth inning of what would be the start of a sweep.
He was supposed to be in the bullpen the following season, but a mountain of injuries forced him to step up in the rotation, starting what became a nightmarish 2023 season. Since then, Schmidt has made 63 appearances through his season-ending elbow surgery in 2025, all but one as a starter.
That's not in the cards for 2026, so what can he do to be useful for the Yankees in the playoffs?
Where Schmidt could fit into unstable bullpen
Schmidt adds a multi-inning righty option to a bullpen that has a lot of moving parts. He leaned hard on a cutter-slider combo on Wednesday, but also featured his sinker, four-seamer, and curveball. His velocity looked as firm as ever, something that could be enhanced but didn't need to hold back for 100 pitches.
The bullpen's premier multi-inning righty is Paul Blackburn, who relies on a ton of spin and movement in his profile, making him more volatile in games with shoddy command. He, along with closer David Bednar and lefty Brent Headrick, makes up the team's three highest-leverage arms, but it's wide open beneath them, particularly after Fernando Cruz's elbow injury.
John Schreiber has been effective as a righty specialist in a small sample, so he feels like the leader in the clubhouse as the team's sixth-inning arm, but he might not be playable in certain matchups due to his struggles against lefties. Tim Hill's overall struggles, even if he remains sharp against lefties, will also give pause. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil haven't pitched enough to earn trust in leverage.
There are two ways that Schmidt can be deployed. One of which is as the team's right-handed bridge reliever, as sort of a "platoon" with Ryan Yarbrough (or Weathers, when he returns). Lineups with more right-handed hitters will fare significantly better against Weathers or Yarbrough if the team needs them to come into a big spot to provide some length to the back-end guys, so having a guy with the opposite hand who can fill that role is valuable.
But that role could be reserved for Warren, who's more stretched out than Schmidt and isn't at risk of being removed due to a long inning. I doubt Schmidt would be permitted to throw much more than 30 pitches in a game. That could lead the 30-year-old to be more in the Schreiber role as the sixth-inning guy, possibly pitching in higher leverage if needed due to overuse.
There are a lot of questions about Schmidt as we come down the stretch, but the important thing is that he's back and he's healthy. The more bullpen depth, the merrier.

It was a game the Yankees deemed they had to have, so they were going to do whatever they could to run it down.
Down 2-0 in Minnesota in the seventh inning on Wednesday, Aaron Boone tapped the gas pedal. With runners on second and third in a game that was a swing away from getting out of reach, he brought in Brent Headrick for the 77th time this season, which trails only Toronto’s Mason Fluharty for most appearances in the majors. Headrick escaped — and then returned to the mound for the eighth, now up to 75 ⅔ innings on the year.
That effort appeared to pay off in the ninth, when Anthony Volpe’s two-run double tied it, and led to more burn on the Yankees tires: Boone went to Paul Blackburn (81 ⅔ innings and counting in his first full season as a reliever) for a scoreless bottom of the ninth, and then David Bednar (66 ⅓ innings, plus another four pressure-packed frames during the World Baseball Classic) for the 10th — and, as neither team could separate itself, the 11th, too. So with less than two weeks before the start of the postseason, Bednar added 26 more pitches to his odometer.
Boone’s management was understandable: The Yankees are trying to keep pace with the Rays and can speak from experience how significant winning the division and clinching the first-round bye can be.

On the offensive front, the New York Yankees have a lot to worry about. Pitching-wise, things are okay — more than okay, actually.
Despite a lackluster trade deadline in which general manager Brian Cashman failed to add any relievers, the team bolstered its pitching depth in the weeks that followed. They lucked out by adding John Schreiber, which was essentially a salary dump for the Kansas City Royals, and Clarke Schmidt coming off the IL is another positive.
The Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon was an ugly one they needed, and Minnesota's walk-off left a bad taste, while Aaron Judge had another injury scare. But it was another stellar day for the pen, outside of David Bednar letting up two leads in extras. Schmidt is one reason to look forward to what the pen could be in October, and even if he has a little more rust to knock off, there are a few things to be excited about.
Giving length
Schmidt isn't built up, but he should be good to give a little more than an inning at a time as a reliever. While he only pitched 2/3 innings in his return to the mound, it's clear the Yankees are building Schmidt up to go multiple innings. In three of his five rehab starts, he pitched more than one inning. In two of them, he pitched two innings.
Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick have clearly been overworked. Somebody like Schmidt lightens their load, and soon another starter, Ryan Weathers, will join the bullpen.
More strikeout stuff in the bullpen
The Yankees have desperately needed strikeout stuff, especially in the middle innings. The Yankees have guys who can generate whiffs in Bednar, Blackburn, and Headrick, but that's missing if a starter comes out early. Schmidt gives them that. He struck out two batters in his debut, and despite allowing two hits, he navigated through it because of the whiffs.
Schmidt also showed strikeout stuff in his rehab start. He struck out 11 batters in seven innings. He hasn't had a full season since 2023, but in 2024 and 2025 combined, the veteran hurler had a 9.11 K/9. That should play in October.
No more sweeper?
The sweeper was Schmidt's second-most-used pitch in 2024. It was his third-most-used pitch in 2023. Against the Minnesota Twins, he didn't throw it once. It could be a pitch he's throwing away.
It would be a surprise if he did that, though. Batters hit .210 off it and struck out 33.8% of the time against it in 2024. In 2025, they hit .125 off the sweeper. They struck out 35.8% of the time against it. It's something to look to in future outings.
Potential trade bait
You can never have too much pitching, and if there is one thing the 2026 Yankees understand full well, it's that pitching depth is paramount. It's how they navigated the season.
That said, Schmidt has one year left after this season. The Yankees may want to sell high on him if they don't plan on bringing him back. The rotation should be full again next year, and if they need pitching depth, they have Ryan Weathers and Will Warren.
This season could be a showcase of sorts for Schmidt. The veteran showing he can finish out the season could be a selling point in the winter.
Chances are, Schmidt won't be able to start next year anyway, and if he does, he won't have a full workload since he needs to build back up. The last time he pitched more than 150 innings was in 2023. That said, the Yankees could use this as an opportunity to deal an oft-injured pitcher and fill another area of need.

“I am beyond thankful for all the support and it was really fun to play,” Alonso said after homering in the Orioles’ 7-1 win over the Mets on Wednesday at Citi Field to complete a three-game sweep.
“I feel like New York will always be a place where it feels like homecoming – it doesn’t matter whether it’s here or at Yankee Stadium. The whole city of New York is meaningful to us.”
It’s certainly understandable that Alonso would feel the love at Citi Field from Mets fans since it would appear most team supporters wish the team did not leave him leave.
There isn’t that history with the Yankees, though, and he’s performed quite well against them in his career.
Alonso, spanning his seven seasons with the Mets and this first with the AL East rival Orioles, owns a career .253/.333/.558 slash line with 14 homers and 35 RBIs in his career against the Bronx Bombers.
At Yankee Stadium, Alonso has hit .247/.312/.600 with nine homers and 21 RBIs in 23 games.
Alonso went 5-for-14 with two solo homers in the Yankees’ four-game sweep in The Bronx from May 1-4 this year.
With just 42 games against the Yankees under his belt, the first baseman is statistically averaging a homer in every three-game set and five RBIs every six games.
When he and the Orioles visit Yankee Stadium for a season-ending series next weekend, it’s possible it could matter for both teams.
The Yankees are not likely to win the AL East but they could be in the race still dependent on how next week’s four-game set with the Rays plays out in The Bronx.
They also could be battling the Red Sox, who they lead by six games while owning the tiebreaker, for the top wild-card spot.
The Orioles (75-78) are 2 1/2 games out of the third and final Wild Card spot and would need to pass three teams to return to the postseason for the first time since 2024.

MINNEAPOLIS — Anthony Volpe bateó con tanta fuerza que perdió el equilibrio, convencido de que la pelota se había ido fuera. En cambio, rebotó contra el muro alto del centro-derecha, un doble de dos carreras que igualó el marcador para los Yankees con dos outs en la novena entrada. Durante un momento intenso y emocionante el miércoles, Nueva York parecía dispuesta a llevarse la barrida.
Lo que vino después fueron cuatro entradas más en las que el equipo llegaba hasta la puerta y se negaba a cruzarla. Los Yankees se pusieron por delante en la décima. Volvieron a hacerlo en la undécima. Llenaron las bases sin outs en la duodécima. Cada vez acababan con un empate o con una remontada desperdiciada.
Un viaje que debería haber acabado con una barrida acabó poniendo de manifiesto el único punto débil que un aspirante al título no puede permitirse arrastrar hasta octubre. No se trató de un colapso del bullpen ni de un rebote desafortunado. Fue la alineación de los Yankees la que no paraba de preparar la mesa, pero nunca se sentaba a comer.
La culpa final recayó en un novato que no se la merecía él solo.
Los Minnesota Twins vencieron a los Yankees por 5-4 en 13 entradas, poniendo fin a ese partido maratoniano con un sencillo de Victor Caratini en la primera base que rebotó en el montículo y se coló por debajo del guante de George Lombard Jr. en la segunda base. Con esta derrota, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-64, a cuatro partidos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en los playoffs, pero el título de la división y la exención de la primera ronda se les están escapando.
Una remontada que no llevó a ninguna parte
Nueva York había sumado cuatro hits en ocho entradas y perdía por 2-0, mientras que el lanzador diestro de los Twins, Zebby Matthews, había ponchado a ocho. Entonces llegó la novena entrada. Lombard conectó un sencillo, Paul Goldschmidt le siguió y el corredor suplente José Caballero preparó el terreno para Volpe.
Volpe impulsó las dos carreras, lo que le supuso al cerrador de los Twins, Yoendrys Gómez, su primer salvamento fallido del año y obligó a jugar entradas extras.
Ali Sánchez impulsó al corredor automático con un sencillo en la décima entrada, dando a los Yankees su primera ventaja. Luke Keaschall respondió con un sencillo que empató el partido ante David Bednar. Un fly de sacrificio de Caballero puso a Nueva York por delante en la undécima. Royce Lewis igualó el marcador. Dos ventajas, dos respuestas inmediatas.
La entrada que dará que hablar
La 12.ª es la entrada que los aficionados volverán a ver una y otra vez. Los Yankees llenaron las bases sin outs, la situación que debería haber sentenciado el partido. Pero no sacaron nada de ella.
Heliot Ramos, que bateaba en el turno de Aaron Judge, mandó una bola corta hacia el montículo. Travis Adams la convirtió en una doble jugada 1-2-3. Sánchez se fue con un strikeout, dejando a otros dos en base. Los Yankees acabaron con 7 de 30 con corredores en posición de anotar.
El juez se marcha y el ataque se queda con pocos jugadores
Judge se retiró en la sexta entrada por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha que empezó a notar en la primera entrada. Falló dos veces y no volvió al campo, solo siete partidos después de una ausencia de 99 días. Por eso Ramos estaba bateando en su lugar.
El entrenador Aaron Boone describió la noche como una oportunidad perdida, no como un partido robado, y sus palabras reflejaban la importancia del momento en el calendario.
«Obviamente, muchas cosas buenas, pero no las suficientes», dijo Boone. «Ha sido un golpe duro, claro, cuando tenías la oportunidad de barrer la serie y justo antes de un día de descanso. Pero tenemos que superarlo y prepararnos para enfrentarnos a un buen equipo de los Diamondbacks».
Al final del partido, Boone no se anduvo con rodeos con Lombard, pero tampoco lo machacó.
Boone reconoció que la bola de Caratini rebotó en el montículo, pero fue una jugada que Lombard «se espera que haga y sabemos que es capaz de hacer».
Rodón lo da todo en octubre, pero no saca nada a cambio
Carlos Rodón le dio a los Yankees el comienzo que necesita una rotación en la postemporada y vio cómo se esfumaba. El zurdo encajó dos carreras en seis entradas, ampliando su récord de la franquicia a 25 salidas consecutivas en las que ha encajado tres carreras o menos. Lanzó 102 lanzamientos, su máximo de la temporada, y bajó su promedio de carreras limpias a 2,95.
«Empecé un poco lento, un poco tenso», dijo Rodon. «Me fui soltando en las siguientes entradas, así que eso estuvo bien».
Clarke Schmidt hizo su tan esperado regreso en la séptima entrada, ponchando a dos antes de que Brent Headrick dejara a dos en base. El bullpen corrió una maratón que la alineación nunca supo recompensar.
Una primicia para el club que no se veía desde 1991
Este es el dato que pocos destacarán. Ha sido la primera derrota de los Yankees tras ir ganando varias veces en entradas extras desde el 5 de mayo de 1991, en Seattle, es decir, en un lapso de más de 34 años. También fue su octava derrota en la última entrada de la temporada, un récord de la franquicia, y ningún equipo de la MLB ha encajado más hits decisivos en la última entrada en 2026, según datos de Baseball Reference. Ningún equipo de los Yankees ha perdido nunca más partidos a domicilio en entradas extras en una sola temporada.
Lo curioso es que los equipos malos no acumulan cifras como estas. Un equipo mediocre pierde en nueve partidos. Solo un buen equipo es capaz de forzar una prórroga fuera de casa una y otra vez, y luego seguir perdiéndola.
Cómo queda la carrera por la División Este de la Liga Americana
Spencer Jones lanzó su propia advertencia, ponchándose cinco veces en una noche en la que se fue de 0 de 6, lo que demostró lo rápido que se castigan los swings fallidos cuando los márgenes se estrechan. En septiembre se lee de otra manera que en julio.
Los Yankees tienen el jueves libre antes de empezar una serie de fin de semana en Arizona, donde Gerrit Cole será el lanzador titular el viernes a las 21:40 h (hora del Este). No se espera que Judge tenga que hacerse más pruebas. Nueva York ha perdido terreno que quizá no recupere y le ha dado un respiro a los Rays.
Los Yankees saben cómo ganar los partidos intermedios. Una noche en la que solo tenían que ganar uno, no pudieron.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

Cam Schlittler pitched six innings of one-hit ball in his latest stellar outing, and the host New York Yankees earned a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets in the final game of the Subway Series on Sunday afternoon.
Ben Rice and Austin Wells provided the only runs of the game via solo home runs as the Yankees (86-63) won for the 18th time in 26 games and lowered their magic number for clinching a postseason spot to one.
Schlittler allowed only Brett Baty’s double with two outs in the fifth. It was the third time in his 45 career starts that Schlittler allowed one hit and the second time this season.
Schlittler struck out eight and walked two. He moved into a tie with Milwaukee’s Jacob Misiorowski for the major league lead by lowering his ERA to 1.95 ERA.
Schlittler threw 60 of 94 pitches for strikes and ended his outing after taking Bo Bichette’s comebacker off the back of his right leg. The ball deflected to catcher Wells, who threw to Luis Garcia Jr. at first base to complete the out.
Afterwards, Schlittler headed straight to the clubhouse but seemed fine.
Rice slugged his third career leadoff homer and Wells homered in the third off Mets starter Christian Scott (4-5).
Scott allowed two runs on three hits in six innings. The right-hander struck out Aaron Judge three times and finished with seven strikeouts to go with two walks.
Judge went 0-for-3 and is 3-for-17 since being activated from the IL.
The Yankees’ Brent Headrick tossed a 1-2-3 seventh and Paul Blackburn got Lindor on a pop-up to end the eighth. David Bednar stranded a runner and notched his 34th save in 37 chances.
The Mets (69-80) were blanked for the 14th time as Lindor and Juan Soto were a combined 0-for-7 with four strikeouts.
–Field Level Media

The Yankees reinstated Clarke Schmidt from the 60-day injured list ahead of today’s series finale in Minnesota. The team also optioned right-handed reliever Bradley Hanner to Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, and designated Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment.
It’s the end of a long road back for Schmidt, who hasn’t pitched on a major league mound since July 2025 after undergoing Tommy John surgery. At the time, Schmidt was in the midst of establishing himself as one of the Yankees’ best starters, running a 3.07 ERA across 164 innings between 2024 and 2025.
Schmidt won’t have enough time to build up to a starter’s workload prior to the postseason, but he has a real chance to make an impact in the Yankee bullpen. He’s been used in one-to-two inning stretches in the minors, where his fastball has sat around his customary 94 mph. Beyond David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, and Brent Headrick, the Yankees have little set in stone in their bullpen, leaving a wide opportunity for someone like Schmidt to grab a meaningful role with a strong showing in the final two weeks of the season.
The Yankees had to manage their 40-man roster as a result of this move, and Cabrera was sadly the casualty. Schmidt coming off the 60-day IL necessitated clearing a spot on a full 40-man. Cabrera, who has spent most of the season at Triple-A after recovering from a gruesome knee injury last year, drew the short stick. The Yankees could have plausibly transferred Fernando Cruz to the 60-day IL, but instead opted to keep hope alive for a return from Cruz.

The New York Yankees added Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos ahead of the trade deadline, but the big concern, the bullpen, was an area where Brian Cashman walked away empty-handed. In the following weeks, the front office made some moves through the waiver wire, and adding John Schreiber has somewhat remedied their deadline whiff.
This season, Schreiber has a 3.20 ERA in 56.1 IP. It's as low as it is because the veteran reliever has posted zeroes in the run column in every outing that Aaron Boone has turned to him. When the Kansas City Royals cut him loose — most likely for monetary reasons — he was sitting on a 3.65 ERA, and his seven-inning scoreless streak in pinstripes has brought that to where Schreiber has been for most of his career.
One thing about Schreiber is that while he isn't getting the strikeouts he once did, he's been able to give length when needed, too. In three of the six appearances, Schreiber has pitched 1.1 innings. That ability matters as much as his dependability, because the bullpen needed a few more arms to carry the load for Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick — two guys who carried the Yankees through a year-long medley of close games.
His most recent outing in which he did this was the first game against the Minnesota Twins on Monday night. In the bottom of the eighth, Tim Hill gave up a home run to Josh Bell, Emmanuel Rodriguez reached on an error, and Victor Caratini reached base after he was hit by a pitch. Schreiber was then tasked with getting four outs for Boone. He started by shutting the door on Minnesota's budding rally.
In the ninth, after walking Luke Keaschell, Schreiber induced a double play. That inning got a little dicey, though, after a walk and another error, but Schreiber danced around the base runners without David Bednar needing to come in.
A lucky add for the Yankees
While Schreiber has been fantastic in New York, it's hard to credit his success to Matt Blake magic. Schreiber has always been one of baseball's more dependable relievers, and his 3.20 ERA is slightly lower than his career 3.57 across Detroit, Boston, and Kansas City.
Schreiber is actually the type of pitcher the Yankees needed to acquire at the deadline. There was a lot of talk about a blockbuster Mason Miller deal, but what this team needed most was a few veteran arms who can be dependable in higher-leverage spots, so Boone isn't forced to go to Hendrick and Blackburn. Schreiber has been exactly that, and the Yankees are lucky the Royals wanted to save a few dollars with him.
